title: Why Music Gives You Chills
desc: One song, one quiet moment, and a shiver runs down your arms. Why? In this calm, sourced deep dive we follow one imagined listener, Theo, through a single evening of music and look at what science says about musical chills: what goosebumps are, who gets them, the brain's reward system and dopamine, the role of expectation and surprise, why sad songs can feel so good, how songs carry memories, and why every human culture sings. The last part is a long, gentle wind-down to help you fall asleep.
next: Why Time Speeds Up as You Get Older
plan: b01: hook. Theo (an imagined listener, say so) at a small evening concert in an old hall; after a hush a single voice enters and a shiver runs from his neck down his arms. Overview list. Frisson as the name.

b02: what a chill is: goosebumps, arrector pili muscles, sympathetic nervous system; Darwin (1872) on hair standing on end in animals; Benedek & Kaernbach (2011) filmed goosebumps; chills without visible goosebumps.

b03: who gets chills: Goldstein (1980) survey, music the most common trigger; estimates vary widely (de Fleurian & Pearce 2021 review); openness to experience (Colver & El-Alayli 2016); Sachs et al. (2016) 20 people, more connections between hearing and emotion areas.
b04: when music does nothing: specific musical anhedonia (Mas-Herrero et al. 2014); the opioid clue: Goldstein's naloxone test, Mallik, Chanda & Levitin (2017) naltrexone lowered music pleasure.
b05: Blood & Zatorre (2001): 10 musicians, their own chill music, PET; reward areas up, amygdala down.
b06: Salimpoor et al. (2011): 217 screened, 8 scanned; dopamine during chills; caudate in anticipation, nucleus accumbens at the peak.
b07: Ferreri et al. (2019): 27 people, levodopa raised music pleasure, risperidone lowered it; dopamine as wanting and learning, not simply pleasure.
b08: what in the music: Sloboda (1991) 83 listeners; Guhn, Hamm & Zentner (2007); Grewe et al. (2007): not automatic.
b09: expectation: Meyer (1956), Huron (2006) Sweet Anticipation, ITPRA, contrastive valence.
b10: Panksepp (1995): bittersweet songs and the separation-call idea (a hypothesis).
b11: chills vs tears: Mori & Iwanaga (2017); the pleasure of sad music (Sachs, Damasio & Habibi 2015).
b12: music and memory: Janata (2009) medial prefrontal cortex; reminiscence bump; Krumhansl & Zupnick (2013) cascading bumps.
b13: music everywhere: Mehr et al. (2018, 2019); Dunbar et al. (2012) pain thresholds after singing, dancing, drumming; Theo's grandmother's lullaby.
b14: recap, chills beyond music, Theo's walk home; transition into the wind-down.

b15-b20: wind-down: the empty hall, night sounds and slow breathing, body scan, a remembered melody by a lake, a snowy town with distant bells, thank you and goodnight, @end teasing 'Why Time Speeds Up as You Get Older'.
